source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: A retrieval-augmented LM system (query generation, news retrieval, relevance filter, summaries, fine-tuned reasoner, ensemble of 6 forecasts) nears the human crowd on 5 platforms but does not beat it overall.
numbers: Test set Brier 0.179 vs crowd 0.149; accuracy 71.5% vs 77.0%. Best zero-shot baseline (GPT-4-1106) 0.208. Random 0.25. Test questions all after 1 Jun 2023.
limits: Backtest with date-restricted news; later work (Paleka 2025) shows such retrieval can leak. Crowd is a strong bar.
agent_relevance: Best early proof that retrieval plus ensembling closes most of the gap to the crowd; sets the S3 baseline.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) ablation: retrieval and fine-tuning
finding: Retrieval is worth a few hundredths of Brier, and each part adds a small step.
numbers: Full system 0.179; no fine-tuning 0.186 (+0.007); no fine-tuning and no retrieval 0.206 (about the 0.208 baseline); fine-tuned GPT-3.5 swap 0.182. Retrieval plus fine-tuning together = about 0.027 Brier.
limits: Ablation differences are about 1-2 standard errors (SE 0.002-0.003). Prompt search alone gave only a minor gain.
agent_relevance: Expect retrieval to give a few hundredths of Brier, not a jump. Do not oversell search in S3.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) retrieval boundary conditions
finding: System beats the crowd only in selective settings: crowd uncertain (0.3-0.7), early in a question's life, or when at least 5 relevant articles are retrieved. It hedges and is worse when the crowd is very sure.
numbers: Crowd in 0.3-0.7: ours 0.199 vs crowd 0.246 on validation; test 0.238 vs 0.240 (51% of forecasts). Early retrieval dates: 0.185 vs 0.161 on test (crowd still better). 5+ articles: 0.175 vs 0.143. All three conditions: 0.240 vs 0.247 (22% of forecasts). Near 0/1 crowd: accuracy +7% but Brier worse by 0.04.
limits: Selection rules were found on validation and applied to test; the win is small (about 1.5 SE). Hedging blamed on safety training.
agent_relevance: Agent should learn when it knows enough: skip or shrink to the crowd when retrieval is thin; do not hedge near-certain cases.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) ensembling methods (Table 14, validation)
finding: Aggregation choice barely matters among simple rules, and an LLM that reads the others' reasoning (universal self-consistency) did not help.
numbers: 6 base forecasts. Mean 0.1656, median 0.1651, geometric mean 0.1655, trimmed mean 0.1649, USC 0.1691, no ensemble 0.1676, human crowd 0.1600.
limits: Only 6 forecasts per question; trimmed mean here is a custom half-weight-on-outlier rule. Differences of 0.0005 are noise.
agent_relevance: Averaging 6 runs gives about 0.003 Brier over a single run; do not spend effort on fancy aggregators. LLM-as-aggregator is not clearly better.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) combining model with crowd
finding: Averaging the system with the crowd beats either alone. Optimal weight on validation was 4x the crowd.
numbers: Full test set: crowd 0.149 to aggregate 0.146 (about 0.003 gain). Crowd uncertain subset: aggregate 0.237 vs crowd 0.24. Ablation aggregate rows 0.146-0.150.
limits: Gain is small because the model is weak relative to the crowd; needs a crowd forecast to exist.
agent_relevance: The crowd-adjustment idea (later in Cassi's entry) has a precedent: weight the market heavily, add the model as a small correction.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) calibration of ensemble system
finding: Zero-shot models are badly calibrated, but the fine-tuned plus ensembled system is close to calibrated without any calibration step. Binning and isotonic regression did not help.
numbers: RMS calibration error 0.42 (system, test) vs 0.38 (crowd). Remaining error is underconfidence near 0 and 1.
limits: Calibration shown on a mixed set; underconfidence costs Brier on easy questions.
agent_relevance: Ensembling is itself a calibrator; extra post-hoc recalibration may be wasted (Cassi also skips it).

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Bastos, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd
finding: A median of 12 diverse LLMs on 31 binary questions is statistically no different from 925 human forecasters, and beats a 50% no-information benchmark.
numbers: LLM crowd Brier M=0.20 (SD 0.12) vs 0.25 benchmark (p=0.026); human crowd M=0.19 (SD 0.19); difference t(60)=0.19, p=0.850. Equivalence test at d=0.5 (0.081 Brier) passed (p=0.017, 0.040).
limits: Only 31 questions, one 3-month tournament; the equivalence test was not preregistered. Humans were a tournament median, not superforecasters.
agent_relevance: Supports averaging independent runs or models, but the evidence is small. Later larger tests are less favourable.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) individual model scores and bias
finding: Individual models vary widely; a top single model is about as good as the crowd. LLMs show acquiescence (over-predict yes) and the aggregate inherits it.
numbers: Single-model Brier: GPT-4 0.15, GPT-4 with Bing 0.16, Bard 0.19, Falcon-180B 0.21, Claude 2 0.21, Mistral-7B 0.24, Llama-2-70B 0.25. Human 0.19. Mean predictions significantly above 50% though outcomes near even.
limits: Small number of questions (31). Bing access did not help GPT-4 (0.16 vs 0.15).
agent_relevance: Ensemble gain is mostly from lifting weak members; averaging does not remove shared bias (yes-bias).

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Study 2: exposing LLM to the human median
finding: Showing the human crowd median improves the LLM, but plain averaging of model and human beats the model's own update.
numbers: GPT-4 Brier 0.17 to 0.14 (p=0.003); Claude 2 0.22 to 0.15 (p<0.001). Simple average of machine and human: GPT-4 0.13, Claude 2 0.14; updated forecasts worse than the average (t(92)=2.58, p=0.011; t(92)=3.53, p=0.001). Update size correlates with gap: r=0.88 and 0.87.
limits: 186 forecasts each over 31 questions; 17-28% accuracy gain claimed.
agent_relevance: Direct support for crowd adjustment: do the average in code, not by asking the model to revise toward the crowd.

source: Karger, Bastani, Yueh-Han, Jacobs, Halawi, Zhang, Tetlock (2025) ForecastBench (ICLR 2025)
finding: On a dynamic benchmark of unresolved questions, expert forecasters beat the best LLM; the top LLMs all used the crowd value (freeze value) on market questions; news retrieval did not help.
numbers: 200-question subset: superforecasters Brier 0.096, public 0.121, best LLM (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, scratchpad, freeze values) 0.122; p<0.001 vs superforecasters. Full 1,000 questions with combination questions: superforecasters 0.076 vs GPT-4o 0.130 (gap 0.054 vs 0.026 for GPT-4 to GPT-4o).
limits: Early 2024 models. The finding that news did not help is from this one setup using the Halawi retriever.
agent_relevance: Retrieval of news is not guaranteed to help strong models; supplying the market price does. Use the market price as an input.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench LLM ensemble baseline (Appendix E, Tables 16-17)
finding: A 9-forecast LLM ensemble (3 models x 3 superforecaster prompts) was built; aggregation rule mattered little, geometric-style rules marginally best.
numbers: Candidate scores (scratchpad, Halawi set): Claude 3.5 Sonnet 0.178, GPT-4o 0.207, Gemini 1.5 Pro 0.214, Llama-3-70b 0.232. Aggregation Brier: median 0.197, trimmed mean 0.197, geometric mean 0.194, geometric mean of log odds 0.194 (2 SE about 0.024).
limits: Ensemble Brier 0.194 is worse than the best single model alone (0.178) on this validation set, so averaging with weaker models cost accuracy (different prompt sets, so not exact).
agent_relevance: Averaging helps only when members are similar in skill; weight or drop weak members.

source: Karger et al. (2025) scale trend for LLM forecasting
finding: Forecast accuracy tracks model strength roughly linearly; extrapolation suggested parity with superforecasters later.
numbers: Chatbot Arena score vs Brier r=-0.68 (p=0.003), R2 0.47; parity at Arena score about 1406 (95% CI 1346-1633). Compute: r=-0.67, p=0.046; parity at about 6.5e26 FLOP (CI 9.7e25-8.7e28).
limits: Small number of models; wide intervals; marginal significance for compute.
agent_relevance: The base model dominates; scaffolds (S3) add less than a model upgrade.

source: Forecasting Research Institute (2026-01-29) LLMs Are Closing the Gap on Human Superforecasters
finding: ForecastBench leaderboard: superforecasters #1; xAI Grok 4.20 Preview (8 forecasts averaged, X and web search, Python) tied #2 with Cassi ensemble_2_crowdadj. Crowd adjustment beat the plain ensemble by nearly 0.01 Brier.
numbers: Gap to superforecasters 0.017 Brier, about one year of progress. Claude 3.5 Sonnet (Oct 2024) 0.117 vs Grok 4.20 Preview (Oct 2025) 0.102. Projected parity Nov 2026 (95% CI Jan 2026 to Nov 2027); dataset questions Jun 2026, market questions Aug 2026. Exact Cassi scores not given.
limits: Blog post, not peer reviewed; no per-entry scores shown; submissions self-run; extrapolation, not a measurement.
agent_relevance: Main source for this subfield row: averaging 8 runs works and a crowd/market adjustment adds about 0.01.

source: FRI (2026) Cassi entry method
finding: Cassi pipeline: sub-question generation, Tavily retrieval with relevance and recency filters, ensemble of o3 and GPT-5, a second LLM reads the reasoning and writes the final forecast; for market questions a crowd adjustment applies when the forecast differs a lot from the price; no post-hoc calibration.
numbers: ensemble_2_crowdadj better than ensemble_2 by nearly 0.01 Brier; tied 2nd.
limits: No ablation of retrieval alone; crowd adjustment applies only to market questions, which already carry crowd information.
agent_relevance: Template for S3: retrieve, decompose, run 2 strong models, review, then pull toward market only when far from it.

source: Metaculus (2025) Q2 2025 AI Benchmark results
finding: Ten Pros clearly beat the top-10 bot team in a large live tournament; aggregating multiple forecasts was the clearest scaffold feature tied to higher scores.
numbers: 96 bots, 348 questions; 93 compared. Head-to-head -20.03 (95% CI -28.63 to -11.41), p=0.00001. Earlier: Q3 2024 -11.3, Q4 2024 -8.9, Q1 2025 -17.7 (overlapping CIs, no trend). All 10 Pros ranked 1-10; top bot (o3) 11th. Survey of 19 bot-makers: aggregating multiple forecasts +1,799 (95% CI +1,017 to +2,582); LLM calls per question correlate 0.40 with score.
limits: Survey is self-selected and observational; 80% of resolved binary questions were No.
agent_relevance: Live evidence that averaging runs helps, but even good ensembles trailed human Pros in 2025.

source: Metaculus (2025) Q2 2025: model versus scaffolding and search
finding: Model choice mattered more than scaffolding; search provider did not matter in a way they could detect.
numbers: Winner Panshul42: 5,899 summed spot peer score vs 5,131 for the o3+AskNews template bot; used Sonnet 3.7 x2, o4-mini x2, o3 x1 aggregated plus 6-7 step agentic research. TomL2bot (Gemini 2.5 Pro plus work) avg 9.53 [5.15, 13.91] vs template 4.59 [-0.41, 9.6]: overlapping. metac-gpt-4o fell from rank 4 of 55 (Q3 2024) to 82 of 96.
limits: Overlapping intervals; one season; AskNews use had no clear effect in survey.
agent_relevance: Retrieval tool brand is a weak lever; upgrading the base model is the strong one.

source: Metaculus (2024-25) Q4 2024 AI Benchmark: bots closing the gap
finding: Pros beat the best bot team but not significantly in Q4; winners mostly averaged multiple LLM calls. The Pro advantage was in discrimination, not calibration.
numbers: 44 bots, 402 questions, 96 weighted compared. Head-to-head -8.9 (95% CI -18.8 to 1), p=0.079. Winner pgodzinai: 3 GPT-4o plus 5 Claude 3.5 Sonnet calls, dropped 2 most extreme, averaged 6. Survey of 13 winners: 76% repeat calls and take median or mean; 75% under 100 calls. Discrimination (mean forecast on Yes minus No): Pros 44 points vs bot team 26.
limits: Ten bots per team; one-sided tests; survey of 13 winners.
agent_relevance: Trimmed averaging of about 8 calls over 2 models is the standard winning recipe; the remaining gap is sharpness, which averaging does not fix.

source: Metaculus (2026) FutureEval spring 2026 results
finding: By spring 2026 the bot team is close to the Pros, not significantly different; team aggregation of bots saturates quickly.
numbers: 173 bots, 297 scored questions; 99 compared. Head-to-head -1.25 (95% CI -4.87 to 2.37), one-sided p=0.247; Pros better on 64% of questions; 9 of top 10 individuals are Pros. Top single bot -4.51; teams of 2-10 about -2; gain fades beyond 10, plateau near 50. Higher-reasoning Metac bots beat standard in 8 of 8 pairs (p=0.004).
limits: Blog summary; scores not comparable across seasons because the question mix changed. Search providers showed no clear winner (Sonar Pro 3.47 vs AskNews 3.23).
agent_relevance: Ensembling several strong bots gives a gain at team size 2-10 and little more; diversity beyond that is wasted.

source: Hambly, Evans, Schwarz, Phillips / FutureSearch (2025) Bench to the Future
finding: Repeated runs of the same LLM forecaster vary a lot; averaging 5 runs cuts the spread by about two thirds. Agentic search beats a fixed evidence pipeline.
numbers: 20 runs x 18 questions (Gemini 2.5 Pro): single forecasts sometimes below 20% on one run and above 80% on another. Mean of 5 cut SD by about two thirds. Variable-evidence SD about 1.7x fixed-evidence; about 60% of variance from the final judgment step, 40% from evidence gathering. Fixed-evidence runs were more variable than no-evidence runs.
limits: 18 questions only; one model for the variance study; pastcasting with an offline corpus (RetroSearch).
agent_relevance: Shows why S3 averaging works: a single LLM run is noisy. Most noise is in judgment, so repeat the final step, not only the search.

source: Hambly et al. (2025) Bench to the Future: evidence and model results
finding: Evidence retrieval helps a lot versus none; depth-first ReAct search beat breadth-first fixed retrieval; newer models score better; extended thinking helped little. Pastcasting matched live forecasting on a 20-question check.
numbers: Brier: Sonnet 3.5 0.1925, 3.5 v2 0.1690, 3.7 0.1712, 3.7 thinking 0.1645, Sonnet 4 0.1560, Sonnet 4 thinking 0.1597, Gemini 2.5 Pro 0.1611. 3.5 vs Sonnet 4 p=0.0024; Sonnet 4 vs thinking p=0.53. All no-evidence forecasts beat 0.25 but were markedly worse than evidence forecasts. Models over-predict Yes.
limits: P-values not corrected for multiple comparisons; no human baseline; absolute Brier hard to interpret.
agent_relevance: Evidence search is a large lever; iterative search beats bulk retrieval; extended reasoning is not.

source: Paleka et al. (2025) Pitfalls in Evaluating Language Model Forecasters
finding: Backtests of retrieval-based forecasters can be inflated by leakage: date-restricted search returns future-dated or future-biased pages, model cutoffs are unreliable, and human forecasts can leak through retrieval.
numbers: Examples: a search for Nihon Hidankyo limited to Jan-Sep 2024 returned a page claiming a later date; search for 'jan 6' before 2020 ranked US-politics pages; 'wuhan' before the pandemic ranked virology-institute pages. Retrieval-based resolution of questions has a 1-5% error rate (Paleka 2024).
limits: Argument plus examples, not a measured size of the inflation; no rerun of Halawi et al.
agent_relevance: Treat retrieval gains measured by backtest with caution. Prefer prospective tests (ForecastBench, Metaculus) when judging S3.

source: Lu (2025) Evaluating LLMs on Real-World Forecasting Against Expert Forecasters
finding: With AskNews summaries and 5 runs per question, o3 beats the Halawi human-crowd value but is far behind a small set of expert forecasters. Median and mean of 5 runs score about the same.
numbers: 464 Metaculus questions. Brier (median of 5 / mean of 5): o3 0.1352/0.1362, o3-pro 0.1386/0.1389, GPT-4.1 0.1542/0.1509, o4-mini 0.1589/0.1589, DeepSeek-v3 0.1798/0.1761, GPT-4o 0.1883/0.1851, GPT-4o-mini 0.2743/0.2676. Experts on 41 hold-out questions: mean 0.1222, median 0.0196. Text reports expert Brier 0.023 vs o3 0.135.
limits: Crowd comparison is across different question sets (0.149 in Halawi, 0.121 in ForecastBench). Expert set small and partial. Author later changed 'superforecasters' to 'experts'. Direct prompts beat narrative prompts.
agent_relevance: Median vs mean of 5 hardly matters. Frontier reasoning model with news is near crowd level, not expert level.

source: Schoenegger, Jones, Tetlock, Mellers (2025) Prompt Engineering LLMs' Forecasting Capabilities
finding: Most prompt tweaks give negligible Brier gains; base-rate-first and frequency framing help slightly; Bayesian-reasoning prompts and propose-evaluate-select hurt.
numbers: Study 1: 37 prompts plus control, 4 models (Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Haiku, GPT-4o, Llama 3.1 405B), 100 questions. After Benjamini-Hochberg: Frequency-Based Reasoning, Base Rate First, Step-Back better; Bayesian Reasoning and Propose-Evaluate-Select worse. Study 2 model Brier: o1-mini 0.217, o1 0.216, Llama 0.218, GPT-4o 0.208, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 0.207. Base Rate First about -0.011 to -0.016 Brier.
limits: Temperature 0, no retrieval, no ensembling; 100 questions; effects at most about 0.01.
agent_relevance: Prompt-level reasoning tricks are weak; averaging and retrieval are bigger levers. Avoid explicit Bayes-rule prompts.

source: Schoenegger, Park, Karger, Trott, Tetlock (2024) AI-Augmented Predictions: LLM Assistants Improve Human Forecasting Accuracy
finding: Giving human forecasters an LLM assistant improved accuracy by 24-28%, even a noisy, overconfident one; no clear loss of crowd diversity.
numbers: N=991, six questions. Mean error: superforecasting assistant 0.40, noisy assistant 0.47, control 0.67 (control vs each p<.001; assistants differ p=.024 on this measure but not on the main one, p=.391). Excluding one outlier item: 41% (superforecast) vs 29% (noisy) improvement.
limits: Driven partly by one outlier question; control got a weaker model with no numeric advice; no ensemble or retrieval on the LLM side.
agent_relevance: LLM advice helps humans but a noisy assistant also helps, so part of the gain is just more thinking; hard to credit the prompt.

source: Turtel, Franklin, Skotheim, Hewitt, Schoenegger (2025) Outcome-based RL to Predict the Future
finding: A 14B reasoning model trained with outcome RL, using Exa news headlines and median sampling over 7 runs, matches or beats o1 with better calibration but not the market.
numbers: 1,265 Polymarket questions. ReMax single (10k corpus) 0.199 [0.187, 0.211] ECE 0.067; ReMax 7-run ensemble (100k corpus) 0.190 [0.178, 0.203] ECE 0.062; Modified-GRPO 0.192; o1 0.202 ECE 0.093. Ensemble vs o1 -0.011 (p<0.05); vs market +0.039 (market better, p<0.001). Simulated trading ROI about 10% ($52 vs $39 for o1).
limits: Single and ensemble figures differ in training scale (10k vs 100k), so the ensemble gain is confounded; news date errors possible; trading is hypothetical.
agent_relevance: Averaging 7 samples gives about 0.01 Brier or less; the market beats every model, so market price as input is valuable.

source: Zou, Xiao, Jia, Kwon, Mazeika, Li, Song, Steinhardt, Evans, Hendrycks (2022) Forecasting Future World Events with Neural Networks (Autocast)
finding: Founding dataset for retrieval-based forecasting: temporal news retrieval helps, but models are far below the crowd.
numbers: True/false accuracy: best retrieval model 65.4% vs human crowd 92.4%, random 50%. Larger models better; FiD Temporal (top-1 article per day) best on average.
limits: Pre-LLM era models (T5, GPT-2 encoder); three platforms; crowd at close date uses late information.
agent_relevance: Historical baseline: retrieval gain real but small, and models lacked judgment.

source: Paleka, Sudhir, Alvarez, Bhat, et al. (2024) Consistency Checks for Language Model Forecasters
finding: Logical consistency across related questions (arbitrage-style violations) predicts a forecaster's later Brier score, offering an instant evaluation.
numbers: Correlation of consistency violation with Brier up to about 0.92 for conditional checks and 0.85 aggregated; other logical checks give little signal; part of the correlation is that stronger models are both more consistent and more accurate.
limits: Few forecasters; not all checks work; consistency is not accuracy. Only partly read (intro and results text).
agent_relevance: Can add a cheap check in S3: if related questions get incoherent probabilities, average or repair; use as a retry signal.

source: Pratt, Blumberg, Carolino, Morris (2024) Can Language Models Use Forecasting Strategies?
finding: LLM forecasters with news retrieval still struggle; part of the weakness is a bias to say events are unlikely.
numbers: Eight sampled predictions per query at very low temperature; Brier values around 0.12-0.18 depending on weighting by outcome; models guess low, which scores well when most events resolve No.
limits: Small dataset; a high No rate can reward low guesses without skill. Only partly read.
agent_relevance: Base-rate skew: ensemble gains can be fake when most questions resolve No; check scores by outcome.
